es.summary: Conexión anormal entre la vagina y la vejiga, uretra o recto, generalmente por trauma obstétrico prolongado.
key_points: Se produce por isquemia tisular durante trabajo de parto prolongado u obstétrico.
Los síntomas principales son incontinencia de orina o heces y olor fétido.
El diagnóstico se confirma con pruebas de colorante, cistoscopia o imagenología.
El tratamiento definitivo es la reparación quirúrgica, acompañada de antibióticos y cuidados de la herida.
Complicaciones incluyen infección, sepsis y daño psicológico.

pathophysiology: Presión prolongada del feto sobre tejidos perineales → isquemia.
Isquemia → necrosis y desintegración del tejido.
Desintegración crea una abertura entre la vagina y órgano adyacente (vejiga, uretra o recto).
La abertura permite paso de orina o heces al canal vaginal.
risk_factors: Trabajo de parto prolongado o distocia.
Uso de fórceps o ventosa obstétrica.
Episiotomía mal suturada o ausencia de sutura.
signs_symptoms: Incontinencia de orina o heces por la vagina.
Dolor o sensación de presión en la zona perineal.
diagnostics: Examen físico con espéculo y prueba de colorante (methylene blue).
Cistoscopia o rectoscopia para localizar la fístula.
Ecografía pélvica o resonancia magnética para evaluar extensión.
treatment: Reparación quirúrgica (cierre primario o con colgajo).
Antibióticos de amplio espectro según cultivo.
Catéter vesical permanente o intermitente para descomprimir la vejiga.
Laxantes suaves o supositorios para evitar esfuerzo durante la defecación.
Cuidado de la herida con apósitos estériles y barrera cutánea.
complications: Infección del sitio quirúrgico y sepsis.
Insuficiencia renal por pérdida crónica de orina.
Daño psicológico, aislamiento social y depresión.
Fallo del cierre quirúrgico → recurrencia de la fístula.
nursing_care: Evaluar tipo, cantidad y frecuencia del drenaje (mL/24 h).
Monitorear signos vitales, temperatura y parámetros de laboratorio (leucocitos, glucosa).
Mantener higiene perineal con solución salina y aplicar crema barrera.
Posicionar a la paciente en decúbito supino con ligera Trendelenburg para reducir presión.
Cuidado del catéter: mantener sistema cerrado, registrar salida de orina.
patient_teaching: Importancia de la higiene perineal y uso de ropa interior de algodón.
Cómo cuidar el catéter y reconocer signos de infección (fiebre, enrojecimiento).
Evitar esfuerzos al defecar: dieta rica en fibra y líquidos (≥2 L/día).
Necesidad de asistir a controles postoperatorios y terapia psicológica si es necesario.

outcomes: Control de la infección: temperatura <37.5°C en 48 h.
Sin signos de infección local (enrojecimiento, calor) en 72 h.

interventions.action: Evaluar temperatura y signos de infección cada 4 h.
Mantener la zona perineal limpia con solución salina y aplicar crema barrera.
interventions.rationale: Reduce colonización bacteriana y protege la piel.

interventions.action: Administrar antibióticos según prescripción y cultivo.
Educar a la paciente sobre signos de infección y cuándo reportarlos.

outcomes: Integridad cutánea: zona perineal sin erosión en 7 días.
Reducción del drenaje vaginal a <30 mL/24 h en 48 h.

interventions.action: Inspeccionar la piel perineal cada 8 h para detectar erosión.
interventions.rationale: Permite intervención temprana para prevenir mayor daño.

interventions.action: Aplicar apósitos no absorbente con barrera de óxido de zinc.
interventions.rationale: Protege la piel del contacto con fluidos irritantes.

interventions.action: Reorientar la posición cada 2 h para aliviar presión local.
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la presión mecánica y favorece la perfusión.

interventions.action: Proveer nutrición adecuada (proteínas 1.2‑1.5 g/kg/día, vitaminas A y C).
interventions.rationale: Facilita la cicatrización y la integridad cutánea.

interventions.action: Registrar cantidad y características del drenaje vaginal.
interventions.rationale: Monitorea la efectividad de las medidas de control de fuga.

en.summary: An abnormal connection between the vagina and the bladder, urethra, or rectum, usually due to prolonged obstetric trauma.
key_points: Occurs from tissue ischemia during prolonged labor or obstetric complications.
Main symptoms are urinary or fecal incontinence and foul odor.
Diagnosis is confirmed with dye tests, cystoscopy, or imaging.
Definitive treatment is surgical repair, accompanied by antibiotics and wound care.
Complications include infection, sepsis, and psychological harm.

pathophysiology: Prolonged fetal pressure on perineal tissues → ischemia.
Breakdown creates an opening between the vagina and adjacent organ (bladder, urethra, or rectum).
The opening allows urine or feces to pass into the vaginal canal.
risk_factors: Use of forceps or obstetric ventouse.
Improperly sutured episiotomy or lack of suturing.
signs_symptoms: Urinary or fecal incontinence through the vagina.
Pain or pressure sensation in the perineal area.
diagnostics: Physical exam with speculum and dye test (methylene blue).
Cystoscopy or rectoscopy to locate the fistula.
Pelvic ultrasound or MRI to assess extent.
Complete blood count (look for leukocytosis) and urine culture.
treatment: Surgical repair (primary closure or with flap).
Permanent or intermittent bladder catheter to decompress the bladder.
Gentle laxatives or suppositories to avoid straining during defecation.
Wound care with sterile dressings and skin barrier.
complications: Chronic urinary loss leading to renal insufficiency.
Psychological damage, social isolation, and depression.
Failure of surgical closure → fistula recurrence.
nursing_care: Assess type, amount, and frequency of drainage (mL/24 h).
Monitor vital signs, temperature, and lab parameters (leukocytes, glucose).
Maintain perineal hygiene with saline solution and apply barrier cream.
Position patient supine with slight Trendelenburg to reduce pressure.
Catheter care: keep system closed, record urine output.
patient_teaching: Importance of perineal hygiene and use of cotton underwear.
How to care for the catheter and recognize infection signs (fever, redness).
Avoid straining during defecation: high‑fiber diet and fluids (≥2 L/day).
Need to attend postoperative follow‑ups and psychological therapy if necessary.

outcomes: Control of infection: temperature <37.5°C within 48 h.
No local infection signs (redness, heat) within 72 h.

interventions.action: Check temperature and infection signs every 4 h.
Keep perineal area clean with saline and apply barrier cream.
interventions.rationale: Reduces bacterial colonization and protects skin.

interventions.action: Administer antibiotics as prescribed and per culture.
Educate patient on infection signs and when to report them.

outcomes: Skin integrity: perineal area without erosion in 7 days.
Reduction of vaginal drainage to <30 mL/24 h within 48 h.

interventions.action: Inspect perineal skin every 8 h to detect erosion.
interventions.rationale: Allows early intervention to prevent further damage.

interventions.action: Apply absorbent dressings with zinc oxide barrier.
interventions.rationale: Protects skin from contact with irritating fluids.

interventions.action: Reorient position every 2 h to relieve local pressure.
interventions.rationale: Reduces mechanical pressure and promotes perfusion.

interventions.action: Provide adequate nutrition (protein 1.2‑1.5 g/kg/day, vitamins A and C).
Record amount and characteristics of vaginal drainage.
interventions.rationale: Monitors effectiveness of leakage control measures.

summary.0.quote: A vaginal fistula is one type of fistula that is an opening from the vagina to another anatomical structure.

key_points.1.quote: Signs of these conditions can include leaking of urine or stool from the vagina, frequent urinary and vaginal infections, and a foul odor.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Pressure from the fetus can cause soft tissues to become ischemic and cause tissue breakdown and malfunction, leading to fistula formation.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: Pressure from the fetus can cause soft tissues to become ischemic and cause tissue breakdown and malfunction, leading to fistula formation.

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: A rectovaginal fistula is an opening from the rectum to the vagina, a vesicovaginal fistula is an opening between the bladder and the vagina, and a urethrovaginal fistula is an opening between the urethra and the vagina.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Signs of these conditions can include leaking of urine or stool from the vagina, frequent urinary and vaginal infections, and a foul odor.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: These complications are more prevalent in low-resource countries where nutrition is poor, labor or pushing is allowed to continue for extended periods, or cesarean birth is not readily available.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Fistulas can also result from episiotomy or laceration repairs that transcend two structures, such as the vagina and rectum.
